\title{Neural Morphogen Operators: Learning Continuous\\
       Reaction--Diffusion Dynamics from Spatial Transcriptomics}

\author{%
  Anonymous Author(s)\\
  Affiliation\\
  \texttt{email}
}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Machine learning for spatial transcriptomics has converged on a discrete view of
tissue: expression is modelled on a graph whose nodes are the measured spots or
cells. Developmental biology, by contrast, describes tissue as the product of
\emph{continuous} spatial processes---morphogen gradients, diffusive signalling
and local reaction networks. We ask whether a continuous operator of that form
can be fitted directly to spatial expression data, and what it buys.
We introduce \textbf{Neural Morphogen Operators} (NMO), which encode irregularly
sampled expression into a continuous latent field, evolve that field under a
learned anisotropic reaction--diffusion PDE
$\partial_t \vz = \nabla \!\cdot\! (\mD_\theta \nabla \vz) + f_\theta(\vz)$,
and decode expression at arbitrary coordinates. The diffusion half-step is solved
exactly in the Fourier domain, making the integrator unconditionally stable and
the diffusion tensor directly readable as a physical length scale.
Across \NDatasets{} spatial datasets spanning four technologies, NMO improves
held-out reconstruction of masked tissue regions over graph-based and
Gaussian-process baselines, and transfers zero-shot across tissue, species and
sampling resolution. Ablations show the dynamics are load-bearing rather than
decorative: removing the operator costs \AblNoDynamicsDelta{} Pearson $r$.
We stress what the model does \emph{not} establish. Spatial transcriptomics is a
single snapshot, so the learned operator is identified only up to the
quasi-steady-state assumption we impose; the recovered diffusion lengths and
Turing wavelengths are properties of a fitted operator, not measurements of
physical morphogen transport. We frame the contribution as learning latent
continuous operators that summarise spatial gene-expression organisation, and we
report the failure modes---notably a persistent bias towards over-smooth
fields---as prominently as the gains.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================

Spatially resolved transcriptomics measures gene expression while retaining the
physical coordinates of each measurement \citep{stahl2016visium,chen2015merfish}.
The dominant computational treatments---spatial domain identification, clustering,
imputation and denoising---represent a tissue section as a graph over the measured
locations and apply message passing to it
\citep{hu2021spagcn,dong2022stagate,palla2022squidpy}. This is effective and it
matches how the data arrive. It also embeds a modelling commitment that is worth
examining: the tissue \emph{is} the sampling lattice. Predictions exist only where
a node exists, the learned function is tied to one sampling geometry, and nothing
in the model corresponds to a mechanism.

Developmental biology offers a different description. Tissue organisation is
classically explained by continuous fields: morphogens are produced, diffuse,
decay and interact, and cells read the resulting concentration landscape
\citep{turing1952,wolpert1969positional,gierer1972theory}. Reaction--diffusion
models of this kind quantitatively account for phenomena from digit patterning
\citep{sheth2012hox} to Nodal/Lefty signalling \citep{muller2013nodal}, and
morphogen gradients have measured length scales in the tens to hundreds of
microns \citep{kicheva2007kinetics,yu2009fgf8}.

This paper asks a narrow, testable question: \emph{can a continuous
reaction--diffusion operator be fitted to spatial transcriptomics, and does the
resulting model predict and transfer better than discrete alternatives?} We are
deliberately not asking whether the fitted operator recovers the true biochemistry.
It cannot, and we explain why in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep2pt
\item \textbf{A PDE-constrained neural operator for spatial omics.} NMO couples a
  graph kernel-integral encoder (for irregular sampling) with a spectral
  reaction--diffusion operator and a coordinate-free continuous decoder
  (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
\item \textbf{An unconditionally stable, interpretable integrator.} Diffusion is
  applied exactly in the Fourier domain under Strang splitting, which removes the
  CFL constraint entirely and makes the learned anisotropic tensor $\mD_\theta$
  readable as a diffusion length in microns (Section~\ref{sec:operator}).
\item \textbf{An honest formulation of the physics loss.} Because the integrator
  is exact, a naive PDE residual is vacuous. We show the content-bearing
  constraint is a \emph{steady-state} residual that asks the measured tissue to be
  a fixed point of the operator (Section~\ref{sec:losses}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation that resists leakage and over-smoothing.} We hold out
  contiguous tissue blocks rather than random spots, and report Moran's $I$ error
  alongside correlation so that a model which regresses towards a smooth mean is
  penalised rather than rewarded (Section~\ref{sec:setup}).
\item \textbf{A falsifiable interpretability read-out.} Linearising the learned
  operator yields a dispersion relation whose sign and peak wavenumber state
  whether, and at what wavelength, the operator supports pattern formation
  (Section~\ref{sec:interpretability}).
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% =====================================================================

\paragraph{Neural operators.} Operator learning targets maps between function
spaces rather than between finite vectors, giving (approximate) independence from
the discretisation \citep{kovachki2023neuraloperator}. Fourier neural operators
parameterise the kernel in the frequency domain \citep{li2021fno}; graph neural
operators handle irregular meshes through kernel integration over neighbourhoods
\citep{li2020gno}; DeepONet factorises the operator into branch and trunk
networks \citep{lu2021deeponet}. We use the graph formulation for the irregular
sampling and the spectral formulation for the dynamics, because the second is what
makes the diffusion solve exact. Physics-informed networks impose PDE residuals as
soft penalties \citep{raissi2019pinn}; neural ODEs learn continuous-time dynamics
\citep{chen2018neuralode}. Our integrator follows classical exponential
time-differencing and operator splitting \citep{cox2002etdrk,strang1968splitting}.

\paragraph{Machine learning for spatial transcriptomics.} SpaGCN fuses expression,
position and histology in a graph convolution \citep{hu2021spagcn}; STAGATE uses a
spatially regularised graph attention autoencoder \citep{dong2022stagate}; SpatialDE
and SPARK test genes for spatial variability
\citep{svensson2018spatialde,sun2020spark}; DestVI models cell-type continua
\citep{lopez2022destvi}. These methods are designed for domain identification and
denoising, not for predicting expression at unmeasured coordinates, and we adapt
them accordingly (Section~\ref{sec:setup}). Spateo models spatiotemporal structure
in Stereo-seq embryos and is the closest work in spirit \citep{qiu2024spateo},
though it targets 3-D reconstruction and vector-field morphometry rather than
learning a PDE operator that can be transferred and perturbed.

\paragraph{Pattern formation and learned dynamics in biology.} Reaction--diffusion
theory provides the mechanistic vocabulary we borrow
\citep{turing1952,kondo2010reaction,green2015morphogen}. RNA velocity infers
short-horizon dynamics from splicing kinetics
\citep{labella2019rnavelocity,bergen2020scvelo}; perturbation models such as scGen,
CPA and GEARS predict transcriptional responses to genetic interventions
\citep{lotfollahi2019scgen,lotfollahi2023cpa,roohani2024gears}. None of these
carries an explicit spatial operator, which is the gap we address.

% =====================================================================
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
% =====================================================================

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_overview.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{Neural Morphogen Operator.} Irregularly sampled expression is
  encoded into a continuous latent field, evolved under a learned anisotropic
  reaction--diffusion PDE, and decoded at arbitrary coordinates. The decoder does
  not receive coordinates, so all spatial structure must pass through the field
  and hence through the operator.}
  \label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

Let a tissue section provide $N$ measurements $\{(\vp_i, \vg_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ with
positions $\vp_i \in \R^2$ (isotropically normalised to $[-1,1]^2$) and expression
$\vg_i \in \R^G$. We posit a latent field $\vz : \R^2 \to \R^C$ and factor the
model as encode--evolve--decode (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}).

\subsection{Spatial encoder}

Irregular sampling is handled by $L$ kernel-integral layers on a $k$-NN graph
\citep{li2020gno},
\begin{equation}
\vz_i^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\!\Big( W \vz_i^{(\ell)}
   + \tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(i)|}\!\!\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)}\!\!
     \kappa_\theta(\vp_j - \vp_i)\odot \vz_j^{(\ell)} \Big),
\end{equation}
where $\kappa_\theta$ maps a \emph{relative} displacement to a per-channel gain.
Depending only on geometry, not on node identity, is what allows an encoder fitted
to one lattice to be evaluated on another.

The resulting features are then splatted onto a regular $H\times W$ lattice by a
Nadaraya--Watson estimator with a learnable bandwidth, producing both a field and
an \emph{occupancy} map $\omega$ recording where measurements actually exist. The
occupancy channel matters: in the masked-region task the model must distinguish
"tissue with no signal" from "no measurement here". A short stack of spectral
(FNO) blocks \citep{li2021fno} then refines the field.

\subsection{The morphogen operator}
\label{sec:operator}

The field evolves under
\begin{equation}
\frac{\partial \vz}{\partial t}
  = \nabla \!\cdot\! \big(\mD_\theta \nabla \vz\big) + f_\theta(\vz),
\label{eq:pde}
\end{equation}
with a per-channel symmetric positive-definite diffusion tensor
$\mD_c = L_c L_c^\top + \varepsilon I$ ($L_c$ lower triangular, so positive
definiteness is structural rather than penalised) and a pointwise reaction network
$f_\theta$ implemented as $1\times1$ convolutions with a $\tanh$-bounded output and
learnable per-channel gain.

\paragraph{Exact spectral diffusion.} Equation~\eqref{eq:pde} is stiff: the
diffusion operator has eigenvalues scaling as $-|\vk|^2$, so an explicit scheme
needs $\Delta t = O(h^2/\|\mD\|)$. For constant-coefficient anisotropic diffusion
the operator is diagonal in the Fourier basis, so the diffusive evolution over
$\tau$ is available in closed form,
\begin{equation}
E_c(\tau) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\,
   \exp\!\big(-\vk^\top \mD_c \vk\, \tau\big)\, \mathcal{F}.
\label{eq:expstep}
\end{equation}
We combine this with a midpoint reaction update under Strang splitting
\citep{strang1968splitting},
$\vz \leftarrow E(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2})\,\vz$;
$\vz \leftarrow \vz + \Delta t\,\mathrm{RK2}[f_\theta](\vz)$;
$\vz \leftarrow E(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2})\,\vz$,
which is second-order accurate. Two consequences matter. First, since
$\vk^\top \mD_c \vk \ge 0$, the multiplier in \eqref{eq:expstep} lies in $(0,1]$
for every $\Delta t$: the diffusive channel is \textbf{unconditionally stable}
regardless of what the optimiser does to $\theta$. Empirically, rollouts remain
bounded for $10^3$ steps, two orders of magnitude beyond the training horizon.
Second, $\mD_c$ is interpretable---its eigenvalues are squared diffusion lengths
per unit pseudo-time, convertible to microns through the stored coordinate scale.

\subsection{Decoder}

Predictions are obtained by bilinear interpolation of the evolved field at any
continuous coordinate followed by an MLP. \emph{The decoder receives no positional
input.} This is a deliberate constraint: given coordinates, the decoder could
memorise a coordinate-to-expression map and render the dynamics ornamental, and
every ablation in Section~\ref{sec:ablations} would become uninterpretable.

\subsection{Objectives}
\label{sec:losses}

The objective combines reconstruction (MSE plus a per-gene Pearson term, since
correlation of the \emph{spatial pattern} is the quantity of scientific interest),
a weak Dirichlet-energy smoothness prior, and three physics terms.

\paragraph{What a physics loss can mean here.} Because the integrator solves
\eqref{eq:pde} essentially exactly, the residual $\|\partial_t\vz - \mathrm{RHS}\|$
evaluated along the model's own trajectory is zero up to splitting error. Imposing
it would penalise the integrator, not the model. The constraint that carries content
is that the \emph{measured configuration should be a near-stationary state} of the
learned operator:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDE}} = \big\| \nabla\!\cdot\!(\mD_\theta \nabla \vz_T)
  + f_\theta(\vz_T) \big\|^2 .
\label{eq:steady}
\end{equation}
This is the correct formalisation of the quasi-steady-state assumption for adult
tissue, and it constrains $\mD_\theta$ and $f_\theta$ jointly.
We add a \emph{mass} term penalising the spatial mean of $f_\theta(\vz)$---spectral
diffusion conserves the $\vk=0$ mode exactly, so any drift in total latent mass is
attributable to the reaction---and a \emph{Jacobian} hinge on
$\|\partial f_\theta/\partial \vz\|_2$ that bounds the local Lipschitz constant,
estimated by power iteration on sampled pixels. A splitting-consistency term keeps
$\Delta t$ in the regime where the second-order scheme is faithful.

\subsection{Interpretability: dispersion analysis}
\label{sec:interpretability}

Linearising \eqref{eq:pde} about a homogeneous state $\vz^*$ gives, for spatial
mode $\vk$,
$\partial_t \delta\vz_{\vk} = (\mJ(\vz^*) - \vk^\top\!\mD\vk)\,\delta\vz_{\vk}$
with $\mJ = \partial f_\theta/\partial\vz|_{\vz^*}$. The quantity
$\max\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{spec}(\mJ - |\vk|^2\mD)$ as a function of $|\vk|$ is the
dispersion relation of the \emph{learned} operator: positive growth at finite
$|\vk|$ with decay at $\vk=0$ is the classical Turing signature, and its peak
identifies a characteristic wavelength. Because $\mD$ is anisotropic we maximise
over orientations of $\vk$. This is a quantitative, falsifiable statement about
what the model has inferred, not a post-hoc visualisation.

% =====================================================================
\section{Data}
% =====================================================================

We use \NDatasets{} processed spatial sections spanning four technologies plus one
non-spatial perturbation dataset (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}). All are public. Raw
sequencing reads are never used: we consume vendor count matrices, and the
download pipeline records a SHA256 manifest for every artifact.

\inputtable{tab_datasets}

Every dataset passes through one QC policy (platform-specific count thresholds set
from assay physics, not tuned), library-size normalisation, log transform, and
highly-variable-gene selection that \emph{force-includes} all detected morphogen
pathway genes so the interpretability analysis is not evaluated on a gene set that
selection has already biased. Coordinates are normalised \textbf{isotropically}:
$x$ and $y$ are divided by the same scale, because anisotropic rescaling would
silently distort the Laplacian and make a learned diffusion coefficient
meaningless. The scale factor is retained so physical units are recoverable.

% =====================================================================
\section{Experimental setup}
\label{sec:setup}
% =====================================================================

\paragraph{Task.} Masked spatial reconstruction: contiguous tissue blocks are
hidden from the encoder and every model must predict the full expression profile
at those coordinates.

\paragraph{Splits are contiguous, not random.} A random spot-level split leaks
badly---neighbouring spots are highly correlated, so a held-out spot is trivially
predicted from its immediate neighbours, and every method looks good. We partition
each section into contiguous blocks on a coarse lattice and hold out whole blocks
\citep{roberts2017crossvalidation}. Gene standardisation statistics are computed on
the training split only.

\paragraph{Baselines.} A non-spatial autoencoder (the floor), a GCN
\citep{kipf2017gcn}, SpaGCN-style and STAGATE-style models
\citep{hu2021spagcn,dong2022stagate}, a graph transformer
\citep{vaswani2017attention}, and an exact Gaussian process with a learned RBF
kernel \citep{rasmussen2006gp}. Since the graph methods were not designed to
predict at unmeasured coordinates, we give each the same inverse-distance-weighted
read-out head, which is the most favourable available choice for them. We mark
these variants \emph{-style} and do not claim they reproduce the authors' published
numbers on the authors' own tasks. Every model is driven by the identical training
loop, masks, optimiser and evaluation code, so differences are attributable to the
model.

\paragraph{Metrics.} Per-gene Pearson and Spearman correlation across held-out
locations; RMSE; SSIM \citep{wang2004ssim} on rasterised expression maps; and the
absolute error in Moran's $I$ \citep{moran1950} between predicted and measured
maps. The last is included because correlation and RMSE both reward a model that
regresses towards a smooth mean, whereas destroying spatial structure should be
penalised. All results are mean $\pm$ s.d. over \NSeeds{} seeds.

\section{Results}
% =====================================================================

\subsection{Masked spatial reconstruction}

\inputtable{tab_benchmark}

NMO reaches Pearson $r = \NMOPearson$ on held-out blocks against
\BestBaselinePearson{} for the strongest baseline (\BestBaseline{}), a gain of
\PearsonGain{} (Table~\ref{tab:benchmark}, Figure~\ref{fig:benchmark}). The
Gaussian process is a stronger competitor than the graph neural networks, which is
worth stating plainly: for smooth genes, classical spatial interpolation is hard to
beat, and much of the spatial-transcriptomics deep-learning literature does not
compare against it.

\subsection{Learned fields and dynamics}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_latent_fields.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{Latent fields.} (a) Latent channels of the relaxed field.
  (b) Correlation between each channel and canonical morphogen-pathway
  expression scores. Pathway genes were force-retained during selection, so this
  is a read-out of alignment, not of selection.}
  \label{fig:latent}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_dynamics.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{Operator diagnostics.} (a) Relaxation of a latent channel.
  (b) Learned anisotropic diffusion tensors as length-scale ellipses.
  (c) Dispersion relation of the linearised operator. (d) Distribution of
  diffusion lengths across channels.}
  \label{fig:dynamics}
\end{figure}

The fitted operator has a median diffusion length of \DiffLenMedian{}\,$\mu$m
(10--90th percentile \DiffLenLo--\DiffLenHi\,$\mu$m). This is the same order as
measured morphogen gradient length scales
\citep{kicheva2007kinetics,yu2009fgf8}. We regard this as a consistency check, not
as a measurement: the model was fitted to a snapshot and the length scale is a
property of the fitted operator under our normalisation, not an estimate of
physical transport. Several latent channels correlate with canonical pathway
scores (Figure~\ref{fig:latent}b), again a statement about alignment rather than
mechanism.

\paragraph{The learned operator is not Turing-unstable, and we report that as a
negative result.} The dispersion relation (Figure~\ref{fig:dynamics}c) decreases
monotonically in $|\vk|$: growth is weakly positive only for the uniform mode
$\vk = 0$ and strictly negative at every finite wavenumber. There is therefore no
band of spatial modes that the operator spontaneously amplifies, and no
characteristic patterning wavelength. Fitted operators were Turing-unstable in
\TuringFrac\% of runs.

This is worth stating plainly because the opposite result would have been the more
attention-catching one. What the model learns from a stationary snapshot is a
\emph{dissipative} operator: one whose fixed point is the observed tissue and
whose action is to relax perturbations towards it. That is exactly what the
training objective asks for---equation~\eqref{eq:steady} rewards making the
measured configuration stationary, not making it spontaneously patterned---so the
absence of a Turing band is the expected consequence of the data we have rather
than evidence against reaction--diffusion accounts of the underlying biology.
Detecting genuine pattern-forming instability would require observing the tissue
away from steady state, which a single snapshot cannot provide. We flag this so
that the dispersion analysis is read as a diagnostic of the fitted operator and
not as a claim about morphogenesis.

\subsection{Transfer across tissue, species and resolution}

\inputtable{tab_transfer_tissue}

Trained on adult mouse brain and applied unchanged to human breast carcinoma---a
different species, organ and spatial architecture---NMO attains
\TissueZeroShot{} zero-shot against a training-mean floor of \TissueFloor{} and an
in-domain oracle of \TissueOracle{} (Table~\ref{tab:transfer_tissue},
Figure~\ref{fig:transfer}). Refitting \emph{only} the decoder, with the encoder
and operator frozen, recovers \TissueFineTune{}: the learned dynamics remain
useful when the read-out is re-fitted, which is the concrete transfer claim.

\inputtable{tab_transfer_resolution}

The cross-resolution setting is the sharper test. An operator fitted to 55\,$\mu$m
multi-cell Visium spots on a 100\,$\mu$m lattice is evaluated on single-cell
Xenium sampling of the same organ. Because all Xenium panel genes are present in
the raw Visium matrix, we rebuild the source with the panel force-included, giving
a shared vocabulary of \ResSharedGenes{} genes rather than the much smaller
HVG intersection.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_transfer.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{Transfer.} Zero-shot performance against the in-domain oracle
  and the training-mean floor, across tissue/species (a) and sampling
  resolution (b).}
  \label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Counterfactual perturbation}

\inputtable{tab_bead}

We perform the computational analogue of a morphogen bead implant: inject the
latent direction that maximally raises a pathway's decoded activity into a small
disc, integrate the operator, and read out the spatial response. The design is
split-half---the direction is defined from a random half of each pathway's genes
and enrichment is scored on the held-out half---with a permutation null over
matched random gene sets. \BeadNSig{} of \BeadNPathways{} pathways show
significant held-out enrichment (Table~\ref{tab:bead}).

\inputtable{tab_perturbseq}

Separately, we ask whether the reaction module encodes real transcriptional
coupling by comparing the model's counterfactual gene--gene responses against
measured CRISPRa responses \citep{norman2019perturbseq}.
\textbf{This is an out-of-context probe and we treat it as such}: Norman et al.\
profiled non-spatial K562 cells, whereas our operator is fitted to tissue. We fit
on the human breast section so at least species and a proliferative context are
shared, report a permutation null, and report the same quantity for every
baseline. The agreement is modest ($\rho = \PSRho$ against a null of \PSNull);
we read it as weak evidence that the reaction network captures generic
transcriptional coupling, and explicitly \emph{not} as validation of the spatial
dynamics.

% =====================================================================
\section{Ablations}
\label{sec:ablations}
% =====================================================================

\inputtable{tab_ablations}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig6_ablations.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{Ablations.} (a) Change in held-out Pearson $r$ when each
  ingredient is removed. (b) Latent-width sweep.}
  \label{fig:ablations}
\end{figure}

The decisive control is \emph{$-$ dynamics}, which sets the integration horizon to
zero so the operator is never applied, leaving an encoder--decoder of identical
capacity. It costs \AblNoDynamicsDelta{} Pearson $r$
(Table~\ref{tab:ablations}, Figure~\ref{fig:ablations}). Had this matched the full
model, the PDE would have been decorative and the central claim of this paper
would fail; we report it first for that reason. Removing diffusion
(\AblNoDiffusionDelta) and the reaction term (\AblNoReactionDelta) are both
harmful, and the two contribute differently: diffusion supplies long-range
information transport into masked regions, while the reaction term supplies the
nonlinearity that prevents the field from collapsing to a smooth interpolant.
Constraining $\mD$ to be isotropic costs \AblIsotropicDelta, indicating the
anisotropy is used rather than merely available.

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}
% =====================================================================

We state these plainly because they bound what the results mean.

\paragraph{One snapshot cannot identify a dynamical system.} Standard spatial
transcriptomics measures a fixed tissue once. Many operators produce the same
stationary field, so \eqref{eq:pde} is identified only up to the quasi-steady-state
assumption we impose through \eqref{eq:steady} and up to the inductive bias of the
architecture. Reported diffusion lengths and Turing wavelengths characterise the
\emph{fitted operator}; they are not measurements of morphogen transport, and we
have no way to falsify them against ground-truth kinetics in these data. The
Stereo-seq developmental series is the only dataset here with a genuine temporal
axis, and even there consecutive stages are different embryos, so cross-stage
comparison is distributional rather than per-cell.

\paragraph{Latent, not molecular.} The operator acts on a learned latent field.
Correlations between latent channels and morphogen pathway scores show alignment;
they do not identify a channel \emph{as} SHH or BMP. We deliberately avoid that
language.

\paragraph{Over-smoothing persists.} Predicted maps are systematically smoother
than measured ones: predicted Moran's $I$ ($\NMOMoranPred$) substantially exceeds
the measured value ($\MoranTrue$). NMO reduces this discrepancy relative to
baselines but does not remove it. Any downstream use that depends on sharp
boundaries---rare cell-type niches, tumour margins---should treat these
predictions cautiously. We report the metric precisely so this failure is visible.

\paragraph{Adapted baselines.} SpaGCN and STAGATE were built for spatial domain
identification, not coordinate-level prediction. Our \emph{-style} variants
implement each method's architectural core with a common read-out head; they are
a fair comparison on \emph{this} task but not a reproduction of published results.

\paragraph{Scope.} Single 2-D sections, one section per condition, ortholog
matching by upper-cased symbol (which misses paralog renaming and family
expansions), and modest compute (CPU-scale training). We have not tested 3-D
volumes or multi-section registration.

% =====================================================================
\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
% =====================================================================

We set out to test whether the continuous, mechanistic description that
developmental biology uses for tissue can be turned into a fitted operator on
spatial transcriptomics, and whether that helps. On the evidence here it does:
treating tissue as a field rather than a graph improves prediction at unmeasured
coordinates, transfers across species and sampling resolution, and yields
diagnostics---diffusion tensors, dispersion relations---that are quantitative and
falsifiable rather than merely illustrative. The ablations indicate the dynamics
carry real weight, and the exact spectral diffusion solve makes the operator both
stable and physically readable.

We are also clear about what has not been shown. No claim is made that the fitted
operator recovers biochemical reality; a single snapshot cannot support that, and
the honest framing is that NMO learns \emph{latent continuous operators that
summarise spatial gene-expression organisation}. The most valuable next step is
data that can break the identifiability barrier: dense developmental time series,
or spatial data paired with targeted perturbation, would let the same framework be
tested as a genuinely dynamical model rather than a structured summary.

\paragraph{Reproducibility.} All datasets download automatically with a recorded
SHA256 manifest; every table and figure in this paper is regenerated from run
artifacts by a single command; configurations, seeds and checkpoints are released.
